correctness.rationale: From \(ns(n)=p^2(p+1)\), every solution divides the target and has \(p\)-adic exponent \(0,1,\) or \(2\). The exponent-two case forces \(n=p^2\) because any extra factor makes \(p^2\) a proper divisor while the required aliquot sum is at most \(p+1\). The exponent-zero case would force \(p^2\mid s(n)\), contradicting \(s(n)<p^2\) for \(n\le p+1\). In the exponent-one case \(n=pd\), multiplicativity of \(\sigma\) reduces the equation to \(d(1+ks(d))=pk\) with \(p+1=dk\); coprimality forces \(d\mid k\), and a second reduction forces \(k=d\), hence \(p=d^2-1\), so \(p=3,d=2\). The packaged verifier exhausts all target divisors for every prime through \(5000\).

value.rationale: Prime squares are the first nontrivial prime-power inputs for the collision function in Question 29, and the smallest known non-amicable collision already contains \(9\). Classifying every such fiber explains that exceptional example and proves that any infinite collision mechanism must leave prime squares after a single exception. This is an infinite structural exclusion tied directly to the open collision problem, not a bounded computation or arbitrary parameter slice.
